title: Kubernetes then and now: How AI is changing your application strategy
summary: Kubernetes was built to run containers. Now it's running AI workloads. See what that means for your Kubernetes-as-a-Service strategy and your platform team in 2026.
body_markdown:
#### Short on time? Read the key takeaways:


- Kubernetes has grown from a container orchestration tool into core enterprise infrastructure, and it now runs AI workloads alongside traditional applications.
- AI raises the stakes. The same clusters must schedule GPU-intensive models, enforce security across distributed systems, and operate across multiple clouds and edge locations.
- Kubernetes-as-a-Service (KaaS) helps enterprises keep pace by pairing developer self-service with centralized security, governance, and cost control.
- Platform teams make the difference. Pre-approved processes for developers, guardrails defined as code, and clear cost ownership help Kubernetes deliver value the whole business can build on.


#### Kubernetes was built to run containers. Now it's running AI. That raises the stakes for how you run it.


The same clusters that host your microservices now have to schedule GPU-hungry models, enforce security across distributed systems, and stretch across multiple clouds and edge sites, often with platform teams that are already at capacity.


Kubernetes-as-a-Service gives enterprises a way to keep pace, with self-service for developers and centralized control over security, governance, and cost. Here's what that looks like and what it takes to get right.


### What is Kubernetes-as-a-Service?


Kubernetes-as-a-Service (KaaS) is a managed approach to running Kubernetes, where a provider handles the underlying cluster setup, maintenance, and scaling so your team can focus on deploying applications rather than operating the infrastructure. It builds on core Kubernetes container orchestration with added layers for automation, governance, and[multi-cloud management](https://www.unisys.com/executive-brief/cis/managed-hybrid-cloud-security/) .


Organizations usually arrive at KaaS from one of three starting points: lifting and shifting legacy applications into containers, refactoring them as microservices, or building new cloud-native applications from scratch. Each path has its own tradeoffs, and all of them benefit from a consistent, well-governed platform underneath.


### Why AI changes what you need from Kubernetes


Container orchestration is still Kubernetes' core job, but AI workloads behave differently from the applications Kubernetes was originally designed around. Models depend on scarce, expensive accelerators such as GPUs. They're often large and slow to load, and they have to be versioned and deployed alongside the application code that calls them. A platform tuned for stateless microservices can run them, though not always efficiently or safely.


As a result,[application modernization](https://www.unisys.com/solutions/cai/applications/) , cloud-native architecture, platform engineering, and governance are turning into the same conversation instead of four separate ones. Infrastructure decisions now hinge on whether you can support AI-ready applications, keep distributed systems secure and governed, and operate consistently across hybrid and multi-cloud environments.


#### “AI is changing the role of Kubernetes from a container orchestration platform into the foundation for modern digital enterprises. Beyond running applications, platform teams must now support AI models, intelligent services, governance, security, observability, and cost accountability at scale. The organizations that succeed will treat their Kubernetes platform as a strategic enterprise product, providing developers with a secure and governed path to innovate with both applications and AI.”


Anil Veeramalli, Senior Enterprise Architect, Unisys


### Where Kubernetes delivers value


The benefits below are most pronounced for organizations with the scale and sustained investment to support them, so weigh your team's capacity and workload profile first.


**Portable:** Reduce vendor lock-in and simplify workload portability. Kubernetes provides a more consistent platform for deploying applications across cloud, on-premises, and edge environments. Managed services you build around Kubernetes, such as databases, can still tie you to one provider, so plan for them too.


**Flexible and scalable:** Break applications into microservices built in the languages and frameworks your teams prefer, connect them through APIs, and scale each service independently as demand changes.


**Resilient:** Design applications so one service can fail without bringing down the whole application. Kubernetes restarts failed containers and reschedules them on healthy nodes.


**Cost-effective, with discipline:** Benefit from faster development, better resource use, and retired legacy licenses, which can all lower costs. Realizing those savings takes right-sized workloads, autoscaling, and clear visibility into what each team spends.


### What enterprise-grade KaaS needs


Kubernetes on its own doesn't cover everything a multi-cloud enterprise requires. A modern[Kubernetes-as-a-Service](https://www.unisys.com/solutions/cai/cloud-management/) environment brings these capabilities together:


- **Automated self-service:** Developers launch approved apps, environments, and templates from a continually updated service catalog without waiting on tickets.
- **Integrated multi-cloud management:** One set of controls covers clusters across providers, such as Azure Kubernetes Service, Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service, and Google Kubernetes Engine, plus on-premises and edge environments.
- **Governance as code:** Access rights, quotas, budget limits, and approval workflows are defined once and enforced consistently across every cluster.
- **Security and compliance:** A unified security approach and a single, consistent view of compliance cover workloads spread across many vendors, including the container images you run.
- **Automated delivery:** Continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines build testing and change management into every step, for AI models as well as application code.
- **Cost visibility:** Clear reporting shows which teams use which resources, so each team owns its spend.
- **Support for AI workloads:** Scheduling and resource management cover GPUs and other accelerators alongside CPU and memory.


### Platform teams carry the load


Platform teams feel this shift the most. They're now expected to keep AI systems running reliably, stay ahead of stricter compliance rules, manage a growing number of clusters, and control rising costs. Meanwhile, experienced people who can operate at that scale remain hard to find.


Many organizations respond with platform engineering: building an internal developer platform that abstracts Kubernetes so application teams can deploy without managing the underlying clusters themselves. Automation tools help too, though few integrate multi-cloud security, compliance, and governance as tightly as they automate deployment.


AI-enabled operations can close part of that gap.[Unisys Intelligence Accelerator](https://www.unisys.com/solutions/unisys-intelligence-accelerator/) is built into Unisys cloud, applications, data, and security services. It pairs agentic AI with human expertise to monitor hybrid and multi-cloud environments, prioritize issues before they reach users, and automate remediation, with governance built in from the start.


### What comes next for your Kubernetes strategy


Kubernetes has proven itself. The harder work now lies in how you run it, especially as more AI reaches production. The organizations pulling ahead treat their Kubernetes platform as a product that a platform team runs for the rest of the business. That means pre-approved paths to production for developers, guardrails written as code, clear cost ownership, and room for AI workloads alongside everything else.


Start by assessing where your current environment falls short on those measures. Then decide which gaps to close yourself and where a managed KaaS partner can help you move faster.

## FAQ


Yes, though its role has changed. Kubernetes is now established enterprise infrastructure, and its job has grown beyond orchestrating containers to include running AI workloads, enforcing security across distributed systems, and managing infrastructure across multiple clouds and edge locations.


Running Kubernetes yourself means your team handles cluster setup, upgrades, security, and day-to-day operations directly. Kubernetes-as-a-Service adds a managed layer, so a provider handles much of that operational work, along with automation, multi-cloud governance, and compliance. Your team can then focus on the applications rather than the infrastructure underneath.


Kubernetes gives teams a consistent way to schedule, scale, and manage the compute-heavy workloads AI needs, using the same orchestration approach they already rely on for other applications. That consistency is one reason enterprises are extending Kubernetes into AI pipelines rather than adopting a separate platform just for AI.
